headline: High-risk default file-based interaction: gpt-engineer can write and execute code in a shared project directory while the zoomcamp profile is non-runnable and lacks isolation details.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no shared channel or runnable surface, so direct injection is not evidenced. B reads and writes the project directory by default, and its tool-use pattern writes files then offers to run, so if A’s materials are copied into that workspace they could be treated as instructions. The pathway is inferred, not directly documented.
conditions: IF A’s content is placed into B’s project directory as prompt text or files
IF B parses file contents as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Keep A’s materials outside B’s project directory
Add a provenance banner to imported files
Require manual review before B executes generated code
Use separate workspaces per agent
requires-engineering: add content-type tagging and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no filesystem or network surfaces, while B touches generated source code and can read/write the project directory. There is no evidence of sensitive data flow from A to B, so leakage is limited unless the operator places secrets into the shared workspace. The pairwise risk is therefore small and configuration-dependent.
conditions: IF secrets or regulated data are stored in B’s project directory
IF A’s course materials are copied into the same directory as sensitive files
mitigations: Do not store secrets in the shared project directory
Use a throwaway workspace for B
Separate course content from code artifacts
Review directory contents before running B
requires-engineering: enforce workspace allowlists

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or concurrency surfaces, but B writes the project directory and supports multiple instances with shared state via the project directory. That creates a plausible write conflict if A’s artifacts are colocated in the same directory or if multiple B instances operate concurrently. Uncertainty about A’s filesystem behavior does not eliminate the overlap, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF A and B share the same project directory
IF two B instances run concurrently on the same workspace
mitigations: Assign separate project directories
Run only one B instance per workspace
Snapshot the workspace before edits
Use version control branches per task
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: B’s workflow writes files and can execute generated code, so if A’s outputs are imported into B’s prompt or files, B may act on them without verification. A is a course repo and not runnable, which lowers direct automation risk, but the pair still supports a classic unverified-input cascade from A into B’s code generation and execution loop.
conditions: IF B uses A’s text as authoritative requirements
IF B executes code generated from A’s unverified instructions
mitigations: Require a human verification step before execution
Keep A as reference-only material
Mark imported text as non-authoritative
Diff generated code against the prompt
requires-engineering: add citation and provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: A is an open-source course with no touched data classes, while B handles generated source code and secrets like OPENAI_API_KEY. No residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented between them, so compliance risk is limited to operational handling of secrets if the operator mixes materials. A is cited for its lack of data handling; B is cited for secret handling.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B’s workspace
IF OPENAI_API_KEY or similar secrets are stored alongside A’s materials
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the project directory
Use separate storage for regulated data
Review retention settings before runs
Limit logs to non-sensitive artifacts
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
